design_detail: Meta-analysis of 36 balanced-placebo experiments (34 articles published before September 1985 in eight journals, listed in the Appendix) in which an alcohol-versus-placebo beverage was crossed with an alcohol-versus-placebo expectancy instruction. 144 main effects of alcohol and 144 of expectancy were coded; multiple indicators of one dependent variable were averaged within each study, giving (by the editors' count from the degrees of freedom) 56 study-by-measure units across 11 types of dependent variable. Effects were expressed as Hedges' g between marginal means, signed by the predicted direction, and pooled as unweighted mean g with an unweighted Stouffer Z and Rosenthal's diffuse-comparison heterogeneity chi-square; Alcohol × Expectancy interactions were counted by statistical significance.
can_establish: How often, and in which direction, alcohol content and the belief of having drunk alcohol were reported to change behaviour in balanced-placebo laboratory experiments published before September 1985, and for which types of behaviour each manipulation showed a significant pooled effect.
cannot_establish: The size of either effect in any defined population or at any dose (participants, sample sizes and doses are not extracted; means are unweighted with unreported effects set to zero; no confidence intervals); whether alcohol and expectancy truly do not interact (a count of significant interaction tests in small factorial experiments cannot show that interactions are absent); or effects at the higher blood-alcohol levels at which a placebo deception cannot be kept up.

sample.recruitment: Published balanced-placebo studies of alcohol consumption before September 1985; no databases, search terms or other search methods are described. The authors wrote to researchers whose reports gave effects only as non-significant, asking for fuller results (pp. 347–349).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized factorial designs crossing an alcohol–placebo beverage manipulation with an alcohol–placebo expectancy manipulation. Excluded: studies that manipulated expectations about alcohol's effects (for example more vs less arousal) or about the type of beverage (spirits vs beer) (footnote 2, p. 348). Only variables of primary interest to each study's authors were coded; indirectly related variables were dropped (footnote 3, p. 348).
sample.demographics: Not extracted. Participants' sex, age, drinking history, sample sizes and the alcohol doses are not reported for the included experiments. The text mentions a women-only physiology study contrasted with five men-only studies (p. 352), and describes the three studies of drinking as studies in people with alcoholism (p. 354), although one of them (Marlatt et al., 1973) also tested social drinkers.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the primary studies.
sample.selection_effects: Published studies only, located by an undescribed search, in eight journals; effects reported only as non-significant and not supplied by the authors were set to zero (50 of 144 alcohol and 65 of 144 expectancy effects). Several effect types rest on three studies. The first author is an author of one included study (Hull, Levenson, Young & Sher, 1983; Appendix).

exposure.measurement: As manipulated in each experiment (alcohol vs placebo beverage; told alcohol vs told placebo). The authors rated each experiment's expectancy manipulation from 0 to 3 on three criteria taken from Marlatt and Rohsenow (1980): taste masking, mixing in front of the participant from appropriately labelled bottles, and a significant effect on the manipulation check (independent ratings by both authors, 97% agreement) (p. 349).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not extracted: no doses, blood-alcohol levels or drinking periods are reported for the included experiments.

comparison.controls: Within each experiment: the placebo beverage (for the alcohol effect) and the told-placebo instruction (for the expectancy effect), each compared on marginal means across the other factor.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (randomized factorial designs by inclusion criterion).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level; participant characteristics were not extracted, so moderators such as sex, drinking history and dose could not be examined except post hoc in single contrasts.

outcomes.instruments: Eleven types of dependent variable: aggression, alcohol consumption, physical sensations, mood, attentional focus, locus of control, helping, motor performance, information processing (memory), physiology (heart rate, skin conductance, skin temperature, pulse transit time) and sexual arousal (penile tumescence, vaginal pressure pulse or self-report) (pp. 349, 352–353).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study measures were not appraised. Signs were set by predictions drawn from the literature: alcohol predicted to increase aggression, drinking, specific physical sensations, positive mood, helping, locus of control and external attention and to impair motor performance, information processing, certain physiological responses and sexual arousal; expectancy predicted to act like alcohol except to increase sexual arousal and to reduce helping (p. 349).
outcomes.operationalization: Each main effect as g = (M1 − M2)/S pooled between marginal means and as a z from its one-tailed p; positive when in the predicted direction. Behaviours were grouped, following Marlatt and Rohsenow's attributional account, into illicit social behaviours (sexual arousal, drinking, aggression, being unhelpful) and other behaviours (pp. 348–349).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 22 counts the pooled estimates (2 overall, 4 in Table 1, 16 in Tables 2–9); several post hoc contrasts are added (humorous vs neutral settings, women-only vs men-only studies, physiological vs self-report measures, blind vs non-blind experimenters).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Both authors classified manipulation quality (97% agreement) and experimenter blindness (94% agreement) independently; who extracted the effect sizes, and whether in duplicate, is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Unweighted mean g, unweighted Stouffer Z, diffuse-comparison chi-square; no confidence intervals, weights or sample sizes. Overall (56 units by the editors' count): alcohol mean g 0.18 (absolute 0.35), Z = 5.10, p < .001, chi-square(55) = 136.49; expectancy 0.08 (absolute 0.27), Z = 2.03, p = .04, chi-square(55) = 98.49 (p. 349). Illicit social vs other behaviours: expectancy 0.17 (Z = 2.32, p < .05) vs 0.03 (Z = 0.81); alcohol 0.09 (Z = 1.26) vs 0.23 (Z = 5.42, p < .001) (Table 1, p. 350). By type (alcohol; expectancy): information processing, 5 studies, 0.5344 (z = 3.618, p < .001); −0.002. Physical sensations, 3 studies, 0.6440 (Z = 4.549, p < .001); 0.0450. Mood, 14 units, 0.209 (Z = 3.026, p < .01); 0.061 (chi-square(13) = 22.38, p < .05). Physiological arousal, 8 studies, −0.225 (Z = −1.193; chi-square(7) = 46.48, p < .001; 0.10 without one suspect study); 0.046. Motor performance, 3 studies, 0.6360 (Z = 3.725, p < .001); 0.1230. Sexual arousal, 9 studies, −0.017; 0.306 (Z = 2.861, p < .01). Aggression, 7 units, 0.255 (Z = 1.764, p < .10); −0.131 (Z = −1.194). Drinking, 3 studies, −0.040; 0.523 (Z = 2.870, p < .01) (Tables 2–9, pp. 350–355). Interactions: 7 of 137 tests significant at .05 (5.1%) (p. 354). Editors' calculations: assuming the heterogeneity chi-squares partition additively (55 = 19 + 35 + 1), the difference between illicit social and other behaviours gives chi-square(1) ≈ 1.39 (p ≈ .24) for expectancy and ≈ 4.93 (p ≈ .03) for alcohol; 6.85 of 137 interaction tests would be significant by chance alone.
analysis.covariates: None. Moderators examined at study level: quality of the expectancy manipulation (correlation with expectancy g), experimenter blindness to expectancy, and post hoc single contrasts (setting of mood studies, participants' sex in physiology studies, type of sexual-arousal measure).
analysis.selective_reporting: Analyses excluding the effects set to zero are said never to have changed a conclusion about whether an effect exists, but their estimates are not shown. Helping, locus of control and attentional focus enter Table 1 (by the editors' count 1 and 3 units) but have no table or pooled estimate of their own.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Physical sensations, motor performance and drinking each rest on 3 studies; with unweighted means and no intervals, the precision of every pooled g is unknown.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In balanced-placebo experiments published up to 1985, the alcohol actually drunk had significant pooled effects on information processing, physical sensations, mood (mean g 0.21) and motor performance, and none on physiology, sexual arousal or drinking; a near-significant effect on aggression (0.26, p < .10). Believing one had drunk alcohol had significant pooled effects on sexual arousal (0.31) and on drinking (0.52, 3 studies), none elsewhere, and a non-significant negative effect on aggression (−0.13). Heterogeneity was substantial for several types. Seven of 137 interaction tests (5.1%) were significant.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says expectancy had "strong effects on relatively deviant social behaviors" and minimal effects on nonsocial ones, with alcohol showing the opposite pattern; the conclusion says expectancy increases illicit social behaviours and that the two factors rarely interact (pp. 347, 358). Gaps: (1) the expectancy effect on illicit social behaviours averaged g 0.17, and the difference from other behaviours was not tested (editors' partition chi-square(1) ≈ 1.39, p ≈ .24), so the support for the attributional account rests on a significant result beside a non-significant one; (2) expectancy did not increase aggression (g −0.13), so the claim about illicit social behaviours rests on sexual arousal and drinking; (3) from a count of significant interaction tests the discussion concludes that alcohol's effects are the same whatever people expect and that the balanced-placebo design is no longer necessary (pp. 357–358), although such a count cannot show absence of interaction, and the authors' own finding that alcohol usually alters what participants believe they drank (18 of 20 studies without a prior beverage question) means the told-placebo, given-alcohol cell seldom tests alcohol without expectancy; (4) setting 35% to 45% of effects to zero, unweighted means and no intervals make every pooled g a rough lower bound of unknown precision; (5) the alcohol effects called strong and homogeneous (p. 356) include mood at g 0.21; (6) the recommended alternative, adjusting for reported expectancy as a covariate, adjusts for a variable that alcohol itself changes, which can bias the alcohol estimate (editors' note).

timeline.event: Marlatt, Demming & Reid: balanced-placebo taste-task experiment on drinking in men with and without alcoholism; one of the three studies in Table 9.

Marlatt & Rohsenow, chapter on cognitive processes and the balanced placebo design: source of the attributional hypothesis and of the manipulation-quality criteria used here (as described in this meta-analysis; not read).

Steele & Southwick meta-analysis of alcohol and social behaviour: 8 of its 35 studies overlap with this one; it reported an expectancy mean effect size of .38 for those eight and an alcohol mean effect size of .49 for all 35, without heterogeneity statistics (footnote 5, p. 356).
McKay & Schare, meta-analysis of alcohol and alcohol-expectancy effects on subjective reports and physiological reactivity; on the project's General list, not yet appraised.
Testa et al., symposium report revisiting the placebo condition in alcohol expectancy research; on the project's General list, not yet appraised.

replication.where_it_stands: The first meta-analysis restricted to balanced-placebo experiments, and still the source usually cited for the split between alcohol effects and expectancy effects. Its methods predate weighted random-effects pooling and confidence intervals, so it supports statements about the direction and pattern of effects by type of behaviour in laboratory studies up to 1985, not about their size. Later syntheses on the project's list (McKay & Schare, 1999; Testa et al., 2006) remain to be appraised.

funding.funder: No funding statement printed; the authors thank alcohol researchers who provided previously unreported results (author note, p. 347).
funding.affiliations_note: Dartmouth College (Hull) and Connecticut College (Bond). The first author is an author of one included study (Hull, Levenson, Young & Sher, 1983; Appendix, p. 359). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A modern systematic review with a reproducible search, duplicate extraction of sample sizes, doses or blood-alcohol levels and participant characteristics, a weighted random-effects synthesis with confidence and prediction intervals, risk-of-bias assessment including blinding integrity, and interactions estimated as effect sizes with intervals; and adequately powered factorial experiments estimating the alcohol × expectancy interaction at more than one dose, with blinding of beverage content checked rather than assumed.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Intervention and comparator are defined by the design criterion, but the population is left open (social drinkers and people with alcoholism, men and women pooled) and the outcomes were identified from the included studies rather than specified beforehand.
The restriction to balanced-placebo designs is explained (to compare alcohol and expectancy within the same experiments), and other expectancy manipulations are excluded with a reason (footnote 2).
No databases, search terms or dates beyond a September 1985 cut-off; published studies only. The authors did write to researchers for unreported results.
Not reported for the effect sizes; only the manipulation-quality and experimenter-blindness ratings were made independently by both authors (97% and 94% agreement).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list; only a category of excluded designs is described (footnote 2).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Studies appear by name with their g values and in the Appendix; sample sizes, participants, doses, settings and outcome measures are not tabulated.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Two features were rated: the quality of the expectancy deception (0–3) and whether the experimenter was blind to the expectancy condition (7 of 36 studies). Randomization, allocation concealment and selective reporting were not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Unweighted mean g and unweighted Stouffer Z, no confidence intervals, no model allowing for the significant heterogeneity, and effects of unknown size set to zero; heterogeneity was tested and explored.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The two rated features were tested against effect sizes: manipulation quality did not correlate with expectancy g (r = .07, −.05, .14), and experimenter blindness did not change mean effects (t < 1.00) though non-blind studies varied more. Other sources of bias were not assessed, so this covers only part of the item's intent.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion takes up experimenter blindness, a study with incorrect degrees of freedom (with a sensitivity analysis) and the failure of the told-placebo, given-alcohol deception, and recommends blinding of experimenters.
Heterogeneity is tested for every pooled estimate and explored by type of behaviour, setting, sex and measure type, mostly post hoc and with single studies in some contrasts.
Not investigated; only published studies were included.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Neither funding nor conflicts are stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Six critical items are not met (2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 15), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. This is a 1986 meta-analysis judged against standards written later; the judgment concerns how far its pooled numbers can be trusted as summaries, not its historical importance. It is transparent about its choices (zero imputation, unweighted pooling, the post hoc status of several contrasts) and tests two bias-related features. Citable for: the direction and pattern of alcohol versus expectancy effects by type of behaviour in balanced-placebo experiments up to 1985, the frequency of significant interactions, the low rate of experimenter blinding to expectancy, and the finding that alcohol usually changes what participants believe they drank. Not citable for: effect magnitudes, absence of interaction, or any dose or population.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 34 articles (36 experiments) published before September 1985 in eight journals, each crossing an alcohol-versus-placebo beverage with an alcohol-versus-placebo expectancy instruction; 144 main effects of alcohol and 144 of expectancy were coded from the variables of primary interest to each study's authors.
key_findings.locator: Sample of Studies; Data Extracted From Each Study, 1st paragraph (p. 348); Appendix (pp. 359–360)
key_findings.note: The text says the earliest article was dated 1972; the earliest in the Appendix is Marlatt, Demming & Reid (1973).

key_findings.finding: Effects reported only as non-significant and not obtainable from the original authors were set to zero: 50 of 144 alcohol and 65 of 144 expectancy main effects. Analyses excluding them are said never to have changed a conclusion about whether an effect exists; their estimates are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Data Extracted From Each Study, 2nd paragraph (p. 348, continuing on p. 349)

key_findings.finding: Methods: each main effect as Hedges' g between marginal means, positive when in the predicted direction, and as a z from its one-tailed p; multiple indicators of one dependent variable averaged within each study; pooled as an unweighted mean g and an unweighted Stouffer Z, with a diffuse-comparison chi-square for heterogeneity; interactions counted by whether they reached p < .05.
key_findings.locator: Data Extracted From Each Study, 2nd to 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Overall, the mean signed g was 0.18 for alcohol and 0.08 for expectancy (mean absolute g 0.35 and 0.27); both were significant (Z = 5.10, p < .001; Z = 2.03, p = .04) and heterogeneous (chi-square(55) = 136.49, p < .0001; chi-square(55) = 98.49, p < .001).
key_findings.note: Fifty-six study-by-measure units is the editors' count from the degrees of freedom (55 = 19 + 35 + 1, Table 1).

key_findings.finding: Illicit social behaviours (sexual arousal, drinking, aggression, being unhelpful) vs other behaviours: expectancy mean g 0.17 (absolute 0.40), Z = 2.32 (p < .05), heterogeneity chi-square(19) = 53.27 (p < .001), vs 0.03 (absolute 0.20), Z = 0.81, chi-square(35) = 43.83; alcohol 0.09 (absolute 0.29), Z = 1.26, chi-square(19) = 26.68, vs 0.23 (absolute 0.38), Z = 5.42 (p < .001), chi-square(35) = 104.88 (p < .001).
key_findings.note: The difference between the two categories was not tested. Editors' calculation, assuming the heterogeneity statistics partition additively: between-category chi-square(1) ≈ 1.39 (p ≈ .24) for expectancy and ≈ 4.93 (p ≈ .03) for alcohol; the categories hold 20 and 36 study-by-measure units (editors' count from the degrees of freedom).

key_findings.finding: The quality of the expectancy manipulation (0–3 on taste masking, mixing in front of the participant from labelled bottles and a significant manipulation check; 97% agreement between the authors) was not related to expectancy effect sizes: r = .07 overall, −.05 for social and .14 for nonsocial behaviours, all non-significant.
Information processing (memory; 5 studies): alcohol mean g 0.5344 (impairment), z = 3.618 (p < .001), heterogeneity chi-square(4) = 4.69; expectancy −0.002, z = −0.004, chi-square(4) = 0.79.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Meta-Analyses of Nonsocial Behaviors, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Physical sensations (3 studies): alcohol mean g 0.6440, Z = 4.549 (p < .001), chi-square(2) = 0.20; expectancy 0.0450, Z = 0.305, chi-square(2) = 0.33.

Self-reported mood (14 units; improvement positive): alcohol mean g 0.209, Z = 3.026 (p < .01), chi-square(13) = 12.31; expectancy 0.061, Z = 1.084, chi-square(13) = 22.38 (p < .05). Post hoc, expectancy improved mood more in the one study with a humorous setting than in neutral settings (g 0.67 vs 0.00; contrast Z = 2.89, p < .01), with no difference between anxiety-arousing and neutral settings (Z = 0.38, ns).
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 351); paragraph beginning 'In order to explain' (p. 352, 1st paragraph)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: the four neutral-setting studies in Table 4 average −0.025, not 0.00.

key_findings.finding: Physiological arousal (8 studies; decreased arousal positive): alcohol mean g −0.225, Z = −1.193, chi-square(7) = 46.48 (p < .001); expectancy 0.046, Z = 0.333, chi-square(7) = 16.77 (p < .05). Without one study whose test had incorrect degrees of freedom (Briddell et al., 1978), alcohol g 0.10, Z = 0.91, chi-square(6) = 5.22, ns; expectancy heterogeneity chi-square(6) = 14.54, p < .05. A post hoc contrast of the one women-only study with five men-only studies gave Z = 2.56, p < .02 for expectancy.
key_findings.locator: Table 5; paragraphs beginning 'Table 5 displays' and 'A potential explanation'

key_findings.finding: Motor performance (3 studies): alcohol mean g 0.6360 (impairment), Z = 3.725 (p < .001), chi-square(2) = 6.90 (p < .05); expectancy 0.1230, Z = 0.645, chi-square(2) = 0.98.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Three studies have been conducted' (p. 352, right column); Table 6 (p. 353)

key_findings.finding: Sexual arousal (9 studies): expectancy mean g 0.306 (increase), Z = 2.861 (p < .01), chi-square(8) = 20.64 (p < .01); alcohol −0.017 (positive meaning reduced arousal), Z = −0.056, chi-square(8) = 10.04. Expectancy effects did not differ between physiological and self-report measures (g 0.41 vs 0.33, Z = −0.45, ns), nor did alcohol effects (0.00 vs 0.10, Z = 0.58, ns).
key_findings.locator: Table 7; Meta-Analyses of Social Behaviors, paragraph beginning 'Nine studies'

key_findings.finding: Aggression (7 units; increase positive): alcohol mean g 0.255, Z = 1.764 (p < .10), chi-square(6) = 12.88 (p < .05); expectancy −0.131, Z = −1.194, chi-square(6) = 18.40 (p < .01). The authors conclude that expecting alcohol did not increase aggression and may lower it.

Drinking or desire to drink (3 studies: Marlatt et al., 1973; Maisto et al., 1977; Berg et al., 1981): expectancy mean g 0.523 (study values 0.66, 0.52, 0.39), Z = 2.870 (p < .01), chi-square(2) = 0.32; alcohol −0.040 (−0.17, not significant, 0.05), Z = −0.315, chi-square(2) = 0.30.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Three studies have investigated' (p. 354); Table 9 (p. 355)
key_findings.note: Maisto et al. (1977) reanalysed data first reported by Engle & Williams (1972) (p. 354). For Marlatt et al. (1973), the editors reproduce Table 9's values by averaging that study's three measures (total amount, sips, amount per sip): about 0.66 for expectancy and −0.17 for alcohol, whereas its expectancy effect on total amount alone is about 1.1 (editors' calculation from its F ratios and means).

key_findings.finding: Interactions: 7 of 137 Alcohol × Expectancy tests (5.1%) were significant at .05 (137 rather than 144 because one study did not report interactions for seven measures); five of the seven were significant by narrow margins, and they had no consistent shape. The authors conclude that alcohol and expectancy interact no more often than chance.
key_findings.locator: Interactions of Alcohol and Expectancy, 1st paragraph (p. 354, continuing on p. 355); footnote 4 (p. 354)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 6.85 of 137 tests would be significant by chance alone; a count of significant tests shows only that interactions were seldom detected.

key_findings.finding: Only 7 of 36 studies kept the experimenter blind to the expectancy condition (classification agreement 94%). Mean effect sizes did not differ by experimenter blindness (t < 1.00), but effects varied more when the experimenter was not blind (alcohol effects F = 3.76, p < .01; expectancy effects on nonsocial behaviours F = 5.07, p < .03).
key_findings.locator: Other Issues: The Use of Blind Techniques

key_findings.finding: Among studies with a manipulation check, 59% found that the alcohol actually given changed what participants believed they had drunk: 1 of 12 (8%) when participants were first asked which beverage they had received, 18 of 20 (90%) when they were not. The authors read this as alcohol almost always altering expectancy, so that the design seldom provides a condition in which people drink alcohol without believing they have.
key_findings.locator: Utility of the Balanced-Placebo Design, paragraph beginning 'The above conclusion' and the next paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that for alcohol and the behaviours reviewed the balanced-placebo design is no longer necessary, and recommend using participants' reported expectancies as a covariate when the aim is to estimate the effect of alcohol alone.
key_findings.locator: Utility of the Balanced-Placebo Design, last paragraph (p. 357, continuing on p. 358)

key_findings.finding: Overlap with Steele and Southwick (1985): 8 of their 35 studies are among these 36; they reported an expectancy mean effect size of .38 for those eight and an alcohol mean effect size of .49 for all 35, without heterogeneity statistics.

reporting_issues.issue: The Lang studies are labelled the wrong way round in two tables: Table 7 (sexual arousal) lists Lang, Goeckner, Adesso & Marlatt (1975), which the Appendix gives as the aggression study, and Table 8 (aggression) lists 'Lang, Searles, Lauerman, & Adesso (1975)', a combination that matches no Appendix entry; the text cites Lang, Searles, Lauerman & Adesso (1980) for sexual arousal and Lang et al. (1975) for aggression.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study lists in the text match the table contents, so the values probably belong to the right studies, but a reader matching table rows to the Appendix would attribute them to the wrong papers.

reporting_issues.issue: Effects of unknown size were set to zero (50 of 144 for alcohol, 65 of 144 for expectancy), means are unweighted, and no sample sizes, weights or confidence intervals are given; the analyses excluding the zero values are described but not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Pooled g values are shrunk towards zero by an unknown amount and their precision cannot be computed; cite them for direction and pattern, not size.

reporting_issues.issue: The central contrast between illicit social and other behaviours (Table 1) is drawn from a significant expectancy effect in one category beside a non-significant one in the other, without a test of the difference.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' calculation from the printed heterogeneity statistics (assuming additive partition): chi-square(1) ≈ 1.39, p ≈ .24 for the expectancy difference; the attributional reading of Table 1 is less secure than the text implies, while the alcohol difference (≈ 4.93, p ≈ .03) is larger.

reporting_issues.issue: Multiple indicators of one dependent variable were averaged within studies; for Marlatt et al. (1973) the Table 9 values (expectancy 0.66, alcohol −0.17) are reproduced only by averaging total amount drunk with sip frequency and amount per sip (editors' reconstruction from that paper's means and F ratios).
reporting_issues.consequence: The drinking category mixes amounts drunk with counts of sips, which halves the expectancy effect on amount in that study (about 1.1 on total amount alone); the pooled 0.523 is not an effect on quantity drunk.

reporting_issues.issue: Helping, locus of control and attentional focus contribute units to Table 1 (by the editors' count 1 unit among illicit social behaviours, 20 minus 19, and 3 among other measures, 36 minus 33) but have no table or pooled estimate of their own.
reporting_issues.consequence: These effects cannot be checked, and they are inside the Table 1 estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor inconsistencies: the earliest included article is said to date from 1972 (p. 348) but the Appendix's earliest is 1973; the motor-performance text cites Connors & Maisto (1979) while Table 6 and the Appendix give 1980 (and Table 3 spells the name Conners); the neutral-setting expectancy effect on mood is given as 0.00 (p. 352), which the four neutral studies in Table 4 do not reproduce (editors' arithmetic: −0.025).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the conclusions; relevant when matching studies to values.
